# sysutils_file_attributes (Resource)

Manages the inode flags of an existing file or directory, which `chattr` sets and `lsattr` shows, such as immutable (`i`), append only (`a`) or no dump (`d`). The flags are read and written directly with the `FS_IOC_GETFLAGS` and `FS_IOC_SETFLAGS` ioctls, so no `chattr` binary is needed. They are supported by ext2/3/4, XFS, Btrfs and some other file systems, but not, or only partly, by tmpfs and overlayfs. On destroy, the flags the resource managed are restored to what they were before it was created.

Inode flags, which `chattr` calls file attributes, are not part of the mode: they tell the file system to refuse all changes to a file (`i`), to allow only appending (`a`), to leave a file out of `dump` backups (`d`), not to update access times (`A`), and so on. The resource does what `chattr +i` and `chattr -i` do, for a file or directory that something else creates, such as a [`sysutils_file`](./file.md) or [`sysutils_directory`](./directory.md) resource, a package or the application itself.

## Example Usage

### An immutable file, an append-only log and a cache directory

```terraform
# Keep a resolver configuration that something else would overwrite, such
# as a DHCP client, as written: with the immutable flag, nobody, not even
# root, can change, replace or remove the file.
resource "sysutils_file" "resolv_conf" {
  path    = "/etc/resolv.conf"
  content = "nameserver 10.0.0.53\nsearch internal\n"
}

resource "sysutils_file_attributes" "resolv_conf" {
  path       = sysutils_file.resolv_conf.path
  attributes = ["i"]
}

# An audit log that can only be appended to, and a cache directory that
# backups with dump skip and whose files get no access time updates.
resource "sysutils_file_attributes" "audit_log" {
  path       = "/var/log/app/audit.log"
  attributes = ["a"]
}

resource "sysutils_directory" "cache" {
  path = "/var/cache/app"
}

resource "sysutils_file_attributes" "cache" {
  path       = sysutils_directory.cache.path
  attributes = ["d", "A"]
}
```

### Exactly the listed flags

```terraform
# The listed flags and no others: flags set outside Terraform, or inherited
# from the parent directory, are cleared and show up as drift.
resource "sysutils_file_attributes" "exclusive" {
  path       = "/srv/data/export.csv"
  attributes = ["d"]
  exclusive  = true
}
```

## Schema

### Required

- `attributes` (Set of String) Flags to set, each a single `chattr` letter: `s` (secure deletion), `u` (undeletable), `S` (synchronous updates), `D` (synchronous directory updates), `i` (immutable), `a` (append only), `d` (no dump), `A` (no atime updates), `c` (compressed), `j` (data journalling), `t` (no tail merging), `T` (top of directory hierarchy), `C` (no copy on write), `x` (direct access), `P` (project hierarchy), `m` (don't compress). Setting or clearing `i` or `a` needs the `CAP_LINUX_IMMUTABLE` capability (root); the others need the file's owner or `CAP_FOWNER`. Flags the file system doesn't support are reported as errors. A flag removed from the list is restored to what it was before the resource was created.
- `path` (String) Absolute path of an existing regular file or directory. Must be in canonical form (no `.`/`..` segments, duplicate or trailing slashes) and must not be `/`. A symlink at the path is refused, never followed. Changing this forces a new resource.

### Optional

- `exclusive` (Boolean) Whether `attributes` is the complete list of flags. With `true`, every supported flag that is not listed is cleared, and flags set by others show up as drift. With `false`, only the listed flags are ensured, and other flags, such as those a file inherits from its directory, are left alone. Flags that are not supported by this resource, such as `e` (extents), are never changed. Defaults to `false`.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) Resource identifier (equal to `path`).

## Behavior

- **Create** reads the flags of `path`, records them in the resource's private state, and sets the listed flags. With `exclusive = true`, it also clears every other supported flag. `path` must already exist; creating it is up to another resource. Changing `path` replaces the resource.
- **Update** sets and clears flags the same way. A flag that the resource no longer manages, because it was removed from `attributes` or `exclusive` changed from `true` to `false`, gets back the value it had before the resource was created.
- **Destroy** gives every flag the resource managed (the listed ones, or with `exclusive = true`, all supported flags) the value it had before the resource was created. Flags it didn't manage stay as they are. After an import there is no such record, and destroy clears the managed flags. If the path no longer exists, destroy succeeds; if a symlink or special file now occupies it, destroy leaves it alone with a warning.
- After setting flags, the resource reads them back. Some file systems accept a flag they don't implement and silently drop it; the apply then fails with an error that names the flags that didn't take, instead of showing a change on every plan.

Flags that the kernel sets itself or that can't be cleared again, such as `e` (extents, on almost every ext4 file), `E` (encrypted), `I` (indexed directory), `N` (inline data), `V` (verity) and `F` (casefold), are not supported: they can't be listed, never show up in `attributes` and are never changed, also with `exclusive = true`.

## How the Flags are Accessed

The flags are read and written with the `FS_IOC_GETFLAGS` and `FS_IOC_SETFLAGS` ioctls, as `chattr` and `lsattr` do, so neither has to be installed. The path is opened with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and the flags are read and written through that descriptor, so a symlink at `path` is refused rather than followed and the path can't be swapped for another file in between. Only regular files and directories are accepted; device nodes, FIFOs and sockets are refused, since opening them can have side effects. Changes to the flags of one path are serialised with the provider's file lock.

## Drift Detection

On refresh the provider reads the flags and records what it finds:

- A listed flag that was cleared outside Terraform is missing from `attributes`, so the plan shows an update that sets it again.
- With `exclusive = true`, every supported flag that is set is recorded, so a flag set outside Terraform (or inherited by a new file from its directory) shows up as an extra element, which the next apply clears. With `exclusive = false`, flags that aren't listed are not looked at.
- If the path has been deleted, the resource is removed from the state and the next apply creates it again, which fails until the path exists again.

## Import

The flags of an existing file or directory can be imported by its path:

```shell
# By path; every supported flag that is set is imported.
terraform import sysutils_file_attributes.resolv_conf /etc/resolv.conf
```

Import sets `exclusive = false` and records every supported flag that is set as `attributes`. Since the flags from before the resource existed are not known, a later destroy clears the flags in `attributes`.

## Immutable and Append-Only Files

A file with the immutable flag can't be written, replaced, renamed, removed or hard-linked, and its mode, owner and extended attributes (including ACLs) can't be changed, by any user, root included. An append-only file can only be opened for appending. In a directory with either flag, entries can't be renamed or removed, and in an immutable directory none can be created either.

The provider's other resources therefore fail on such files: [`sysutils_file`](./file.md), [`sysutils_template_file`](./template_file.md), [`sysutils_remote_file`](./remote_file.md), [`sysutils_directory`](./directory.md), [`sysutils_symlink`](./symlink.md), [`sysutils_file_acl`](./file_acl.md), the resources that edit a shared file such as [`sysutils_file_line`](./file_line.md), [`sysutils_ini_value`](./ini_value.md) and [`sysutils_hosts_entry`](./hosts_entry.md), and the resources that write configuration files, such as [`sysutils_sysctl`](./sysctl.md) or [`sysutils_limits`](./limits.md). When one of them is refused with "operation not permitted" and the file or its directory has the immutable or append-only flag, the error says so and names the path.

To change a file that this resource keeps immutable, as in the first example above, apply twice: first remove `"i"` from `attributes` (or remove the resource), then change the file and add the flag back. Within one apply, Terraform updates the file before the flags, since the flags resource refers to it. Destroying both works in one apply: the flags resource is destroyed first, and the file after it.

## Caveats

- Setting or clearing `i` and `a` needs the `CAP_LINUX_IMMUTABLE` capability, which root has; the other flags need the file's owner or `CAP_FOWNER`, and `j` also needs `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE`. Reading flags needs no privileges.
- Not every file system supports every flag. ext4 supports most of them, XFS a subset (`a`, `A`, `d`, `i`, `S`, `x`, `P`), Btrfs a different subset (`a`, `A`, `c`, `C`, `d`, `D`, `i`, `m`, `S`). tmpfs supports only `a`, `A`, `d` and `i` (since Linux 6.0), and overlayfs, as used by Docker containers, only what its upper file system supports, if anything. procfs, sysfs and many FUSE and network file systems have no flags at all. On those, apply fails with an error that says the file system does not support the flags.
- Some flags are only meaningful for directories (`D`, `T`, `P`) or have side effects when set: `c` compresses the file on Btrfs, `C` only takes effect on an empty file on Btrfs, `x` needs a DAX-capable device, and `j` switches the file to data journalling on ext4.
- The flags belong to the file, not to its name: every hard link of `path` has the same flags. Symlinks in the parent directories of `path` are followed, as for [`sysutils_file`](./file.md), so every ancestor directory must be writable only by trusted users.
- With the provider's `root_dir` argument set, `path` is resolved inside the tree, as for `sysutils_file`, and `path` in the state stays the path inside the root.
